source.title: Optimal ridge penalty for real-world high-dimensional data can be zero or negative due to the implicit ridge regularization
source.authors: D. Kobak; Jonathan Lomond; Benoit Sanchez

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; some figure values are only shown graphically.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether increasing dimensionality beyond the interpolation threshold can improve held-out prediction, using linear regression risk sweeps rather than neural networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own ridge-regression and minimum-norm OLS results. It also discusses neural-network results from cited work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures linear ridge and minimum-norm regression, not widening trained neural networks. Its dimensionality sweeps are an analogy to V2, but do not test the same kind of system. Neural-network findings are cited, and the authors explicitly disclaim explaining nonlinear neural networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: minimum-norm OLS can generalize well in highly underdetermined problems because low-variance predictors supply implicit shrinkage. Positive ridge penalties may not help, and optimal penalties can be negative. The authors explicitly state that their results do not explain highly nonlinear neural networks.
record.recipe_differences: Closed-form linear ridge/minimum-norm regression, including a spiked-covariance simulation and real high-dimensional datasets; no neural-network training recipe or standard gradient training comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The preferred ridge penalty depends on dimensionality and predictor covariance structure; in the spiked-covariance simulation it becomes negative for sufficiently large p.

fits_no_version.finding: With correlated Gaussian predictors, aligned signal, n = 64, and fixed signal-to-noise ratio, minimum-norm linear regression risk decreases as predictor dimensionality grows beyond interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm linear regression can exhibit decreasing prediction risk beyond interpolation under suitable covariance and signal structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Positive ridge penalties can provide little or no improvement in highly underdetermined regression; the simulation's optimal penalty is negative for sufficiently large dimensionality and equals −150 at p = 1000.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit shrinkage from low-variance predictors can make additional positive ridge regularization unnecessary or harmful.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2.4 proves an asymptotic equivalence between adding random predictors and ridge regularization. Its simulations show that fixed-variance predictor augmentation eventually overregularizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding random predictors to minimum-norm linear regression can supply tunable implicit ridge shrinkage.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2.6 uses 2000 random Fourier features on MNIST to regress digit values with 64 training examples. The optimal penalty is approximately −80 for the selected 80 training sets with sufficiently large minimum singular values; all 100 sets improve until approximately −35.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-feature digit-value regression can benefit from negative ridge penalties, with the risk depending on training-set singular values.

record.problems: The paper explicitly limits its explanation: it does not explain highly nonlinear underdetermined models such as deep neural networks. Several risk curves and comparisons are figure-based without text-stated exact values; the real-data outcome for one of ten dependent variables is not described in the text.

untested.parts: No comparison of neural-network fits and held-out accuracy on fixed random versus natural labels.
No neural-network width sweep or test-error measurement beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected network comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No dropout intervention or held-out error comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized training examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the supplied claim versions, not denials of the reported linear-regression effects. The unrecorded random-predictor and MNIST results fit no version, so they do not warrant missing entries or V2 verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting fixed random labels with fitting natural labels or report held-out accuracy on either.
Tests linear regression as dimensionality increases, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks; does not test MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10 with the specified training recipe.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with other generalization measures.

rows.subject: minimum-norm OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Swept predictor dimensionality and measured expected normalized MSE of the minimum-norm OLS estimator.
rows.value: Figure 2e shows expected normalized MSE falling as p increases beyond n; precise values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Expected over Nrep = 100 training sets; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The paper states that minimum-norm OLS MSE quickly decreased as p increased beyond n; the plotted curve supplies no text-stated per-p values.
rows.check: The reported post-interpolation risk decrease is supported, but concerns increasing linear predictor dimensionality rather than neural-network width.

rows.subject: OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Swept predictor dimensionality and measured expected normalized MSE of OLS.
rows.value: The paper states that as p increased, OLS began to overfit and each additional predictor increased MSE; near p ≈ n = 64 expected MSE became very large.
rows.uncertainty: Expected over Nrep = 100 training sets; no error bars stated.
rows.note: Comparator to minimum-norm OLS; the reported rise around and beyond the interpolation region is described in text.
rows.check: Linear regression does not test V2. The rising-risk description applies before and near p = n; extending it beyond interpolation is misleading because minimum-norm OLS risk subsequently decreases.

source_check.correct: OLS risk rises as p approaches n = 64; minimum-norm OLS risk subsequently falls as p increases further.
source_check.problem: The value matches the text, but the note misleadingly extends the rising-risk description beyond interpolation.

rows.subject: optimal ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected normalized MSE of the optimal ridge estimator across dimensionalities.
rows.value: The risk of the optimal ridge estimator was close to the oracle risk for all dimensionalities; its gain over minimum-norm OLS became smaller as p > n grew and eventually disappeared.
rows.uncertainty: Expected over Nrep = 100 training sets; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The comparison concerns prediction risk across model dimensionality; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Optimal ridge versus minimum-norm regression measures a regularization comparison, not neural-network widening. The near-oracle ridge curve is a comparator rather than partial evidence for V2.

rows.subject: minimum-norm OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Measured expected normalized MSE at λ = 0 in the ridge-risk sweep.
rows.value: The minimum risk was attained at λopt = −150; the text does not give the λ = 0 MSE numerically.
rows.uncertainty: Expected over Nrep = 100 training sets; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The paper reports that the best ridge penalty is negative at this dimensionality, indicating that λ = 0 is not the minimum-risk choice.
rows.check: The value is an optimal penalty selection, not the stated subject's risk at zero penalty. It duplicates R10 and should be consolidated into a ridge-penalty finding.

source_check.correct: Ridge regression at p = 1000 has optimal penalty λopt = −150. The text supplies no numerical MSE for minimum-norm OLS at λ = 0. Consolidate with R10 as a penalty-selection finding.
source_check.problem: An optimal ridge penalty is recorded as the minimum-norm OLS estimator's risk.

rows.subject: ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-validated ridge-regression MSE using a subset of random predictors with MSE using all predictors.
rows.value: The paper states there was a clear MSE minimum at λopt > 0, and smaller λ yielded much higher MSE.
rows.note: The result concerns ridge-penalty choice on real data, not the neural-network conditions in the claim versions.
rows.check: The value describes a penalty sweep using 50 predictors, not a direct subset-versus-all-predictors MSE comparison as the operation states.

source_check.correct: Operation: sweep ridge penalties using 50 random predictors; cross-validated MSE has a positive-penalty minimum and increases for smaller penalties.
source_check.problem: The operation describes a subset-versus-all comparison, whereas the recorded value describes a penalty sweep within the subset.

rows.subject: ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-validated ridge-regression MSE for each of 10 dependent variables using all predictors.
rows.value: For five dependent variables, the lowest MSE corresponded to the smallest λ tried; four others had a middle-range minimum with limiting MSE at λ → 0 close to minimal.
rows.note: The outcome for the tenth dependent variable is not specified in the supplied text.
rows.check: Supported as a linear ridge finding outside all versions. The text describes nine of ten outcomes; the remaining outcome cannot be inferred.

rows.subject: minimum-norm OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected normalized MSE across ridge penalties in the spiked covariance simulation.
rows.value: The minimum MSE had a clear minimum at a positive λ when n > p or n ≈ p.
rows.uncertainty: Nrep = 100 training sets; no error bars stated.
rows.note: This is the p = 50 condition; no specific MSE value is stated.
rows.check: The subject should be the ridge estimator across penalties, and the size should be p = 50. An optimal positive penalty is not a measured minimum-norm OLS risk.

source_check.correct: Subject: ridge estimator across penalties, p = 50 and n = 64. A positive penalty minimizes expected normalized MSE; Section 2.4 specifies λopt = 31 for this same simulation. No numerical minimum MSE is stated.
source_check.problem: The value describes penalty selection for ridge regression, rather than the named minimum-norm OLS estimator's MSE.
